notes.definition: Evolution is a change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time through a process of natural selection, which may result in the formation of a new species.
explanation: The theory of evolution by natural selection states that all species of living things have evolved from simple life forms that first developed more than three billion years ago. Over this enormous length of time, small changes in each generation have added up to produce the huge diversity of life we see today, including all the plants, animals and microorganisms alive now and the many species that have become extinct.

Evolution happens to populations, not to individuals. An individual cannot evolve during its lifetime. Instead, the proportion of individuals in a population that carry particular alleles changes from one generation to the next. Because the change is in inherited characteristics, only variation caused by genes can be involved: characteristics acquired during life, such as a scar or strong muscles from exercise, are not passed on and cannot drive evolution.

Natural selection works like this. First, there is variation within a population: individuals have different alleles, which originally arose by mutation, so they have different phenotypes. Second, there is competition, for example for food, mates or space, and there are pressures such as predators and disease. Third, individuals whose phenotypes are best suited to their environment are more likely to survive. Fourth, those survivors are more likely to breed successfully and pass on the alleles for their useful characteristics to their offspring. Finally, over many generations, these alleles become more common in the population.

The peppered moth is a well known example. Pale moths are camouflaged on lichen-covered trees, and dark moths are caused by a mutation. During the Industrial Revolution, soot killed the lichens and blackened tree bark in many areas. Dark moths were now better camouflaged, so birds ate fewer of them. More dark moths survived to breed, so the allele for dark colour became more common. When air pollution was reduced, tree bark became paler again and pale moths became more common once more.

Natural selection can eventually produce new species. If two populations of one species become so different in phenotype that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, they have formed two new species. Remember that a species is a group of similar organisms that can breed together to produce fertile offspring. Over a very long time this process, repeated many times, has produced all of the species that have ever lived.
keyFacts: Evolution is a change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time through natural selection.
Evolution may result in the formation of a new species.
All species evolved from simple life forms that first developed more than three billion years ago.
Natural selection acts on variation that already exists in a population; variants arise from mutations.
Individuals with phenotypes best suited to the environment are more likely to survive and breed.
They pass on their alleles, so these alleles become more common over many generations.
Two populations that can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring have become two new species.

keyTerms.definition: A change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time through a process of natural selection, which may result in the formation of a new species.
The process by which individuals with characteristics best suited to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing on their alleles.
A group of similar organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
A different form of the same gene.
A factor in the environment, such as predation, disease or competition for food, that affects which individuals survive.

workedExamples.title: Explaining natural selection in a named example
workedExamples.question: Rabbits living in a snowy area are mostly white. Explain how natural selection could have produced this.
steps: Variation: the original rabbit population had different fur colours because of different alleles (caused by mutations).
Selection pressure: predators such as foxes hunt rabbits; white rabbits are better camouflaged against snow.
Survival: white rabbits are less likely to be seen and eaten, so more of them survive.
Reproduction: surviving white rabbits breed and pass on the alleles for white fur.
Over many generations: the allele for white fur becomes more common in the population.
workedExamples.answer: Variation, then selection by predators, survival and breeding of the best suited, then the allele for white fur becomes more common over many generations.

workedExamples.title: Analysing population data
workedExamples.question: In a sample of 400 peppered moths from a polluted wood, 312 were dark. Calculate the percentage of dark moths and suggest why it is high.
steps: In a polluted wood the bark is dark, so dark moths are better camouflaged from birds.
More dark moths survive to breed and pass on the allele for dark colour.
workedExamples.answer: 78%. Dark moths are camouflaged on sooty bark, so they survive and reproduce more.

workedExamples.title: Deciding whether two organisms are the same species
workedExamples.question: A horse and a donkey can breed to produce a mule, but mules are infertile. Are horses and donkeys the same species?
steps: Members of the same species interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
Horses and donkeys can interbreed, but the offspring (mules) cannot reproduce.
So the offspring are not fertile.
workedExamples.answer: No. They are different species because they cannot produce fertile offspring.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think individual organisms evolve or change during their lifetime to suit their environment.
misconceptions.right: In fact evolution is a change in a population over many generations. Individuals with useful variations survive and breed more; the individuals themselves do not change.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think organisms develop new characteristics because they need them.
misconceptions.right: In fact the variation already exists (arising from random mutations). Natural selection only increases the frequency of variants that happen to be useful.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write that the 'strongest' survive.
misconceptions.right: In fact the individuals best suited to their particular environment survive, which may mean best camouflaged or most resistant to disease rather than strongest.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think characteristics gained during life, such as a giraffe stretching its neck, are passed on.
misconceptions.right: In fact only inherited (genetic) characteristics are passed on to offspring. Acquired characteristics do not change the alleles in gametes.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often say that evolution stops once a species is well adapted.
misconceptions.right: In fact environments keep changing and mutations keep occurring, so natural selection continues all the time.

realWorld: Bacteria evolve resistance to antibiotics: a mutation for resistance spreads quickly when an antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria, which is why doctors avoid prescribing antibiotics unnecessarily.
Rats in some areas have evolved resistance to the poison warfarin, so pest controllers have had to use different poisons.
The proportion of dark and pale peppered moths in Britain changed as air pollution increased in the 1800s and then fell after Clean Air Acts were introduced in the 1950s.
examTips: Use the full chain in natural selection answers: variation (mutation), selection pressure, best suited survive, breed, pass on alleles, alleles become more common over many generations.
Use the word 'allele' or 'gene' and say it is passed on to offspring. Answers that only say 'the characteristic is passed on' may not score the mark.
Never write that an organism 'adapts' or 'evolves' because it needs to. Say that individuals with the useful variation survive.
To decide if two organisms are the same species, check whether they can produce fertile offspring.
Read graphs of population change carefully: describe the trend, use numbers from the graph, then explain it in terms of survival and reproduction.
summary: Evolution is a change in inherited characteristics of a population over time through natural selection.
All species evolved from simple life forms that first developed more than three billion years ago.
Variation in a population arises from mutations.
Individuals best suited to their environment are more likely to survive and breed.
They pass on their alleles, which become more common over many generations.
Populations that can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring have become separate species.

flashcards.back: A change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time through a process of natural selection, which may result in the formation of a new species.

flashcards.front: When did the first simple life forms develop?
flashcards.back: More than three billion years ago.

flashcards.front: What does the theory of evolution by natural selection state?
flashcards.back: All species of living things have evolved from simple life forms that first developed more than three billion years ago.

flashcards.front: What is the source of the variation that natural selection acts on?
Which individuals are more likely to survive?
flashcards.back: Those with phenotypes best suited to their environment.

flashcards.front: What happens to the alleles of individuals that survive and breed?
flashcards.back: They are passed to offspring and become more common in the population over many generations.
A group of similar organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

flashcards.front: When have two new species formed?
flashcards.back: When two populations of one species become so different in phenotype that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

flashcards.front: Why did dark peppered moths become more common in polluted areas?
flashcards.back: They were camouflaged on soot-darkened bark, so fewer were eaten by birds; more survived to breed and passed on the dark allele.
Predation, disease, competition for food, mates or space (any three).

flashcards.front: Can a characteristic acquired during life be passed on?
flashcards.back: No. Only inherited (genetic) characteristics are passed on.

questions.question: Which is the best definition of evolution?
options: A change in the characteristics of an individual during its life
A change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time
The process of an organism becoming larger
The formation of fossils in rocks
markScheme: 1 mark: a change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time
questions.explanation: Evolution happens to populations over many generations and involves inherited characteristics. Individuals do not evolve during their lives, and fossils are evidence for evolution rather than evolution itself.

questions.question: According to the theory of evolution, how long ago did the first simple life forms develop?
options: More than three billion years ago
About ten thousand years ago
About three million years ago
About 6000 years ago
markScheme: 1 mark: more than three billion years ago
questions.explanation: The theory states that all species evolved from simple life forms that first developed more than three billion years ago. Three million years is far too recent.

questions.question: What is the name of the process in which individuals best suited to their environment survive and reproduce?
options: Selective breeding
Genetic engineering
Natural selection
Cloning
markScheme: 1 mark: natural selection
questions.explanation: In natural selection the environment 'selects' which individuals survive. In selective breeding humans choose which individuals breed. Genetic engineering and cloning are human techniques.

questions.question: Which statement describes a species?
options: Organisms that live in the same habitat
Organisms that eat the same food
Organisms that look exactly alike
Organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring
markScheme: 1 mark: organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring
questions.explanation: The test of a species is whether organisms can breed together to produce fertile offspring. Members of a species can look different, and different species often share habitats and food.

questions.question: What is the original source of the variation on which natural selection acts?
options: Mutations
Competition
Predators
Changes in the environment
markScheme: 1 mark: mutations
questions.explanation: New alleles arise by mutation. Competition, predators and environmental change are selection pressures: they decide which variants survive but do not create them.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the result of breeding a horse with a zebra.
What does Figure 1 show about horses and zebras?

figure.svg: <svg stroke-width="1.5" viewBox="0 0 400 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif"><rect x="20" y="20" width="140" height="44" rx="6" fill="#fde68a" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor"/><text x="90" y="46.6" font-size="13" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">Horse</text><text x="200" y="48" font-size="20" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">×</text><rect x="240" y="20" width="140" height="44" rx="6" fill="#e5e7eb" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor"/><text x="310" y="46.6" font-size="13" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">Zebra</text><line x1="90" y1="64" x2="90" y2="90" stroke="currentColor"/><line x1="310" y1="64" x2="310" y2="90" stroke="currentColor"/><line x1="90" y1="90" x2="310" y2="90" stroke="currentColor"/><line x1="200" y1="90" x2="200" y2="120" stroke="currentColor"/><line x1="200" y1="120" x2="196.1" y2="111.9" stroke="currentColor"/><line x1="200" y1="120" x2="203.9" y2="111.9" stroke="currentColor"/><rect x="110" y="122" width="180" height="60" rx="6" fill="#c4b5fd" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor"/><text x="200" y="148.6" font-size="13" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">Zorse</text><text x="200" y="164.6" font-size="13" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">(cannot produce offspring)</text></svg>

options: Horses and zebras are the same species
Zorses are a new species
Horses and zebras are different species
Natural selection cannot act on zebras
markScheme: 1 mark: horses and zebras are different species
questions.explanation: Members of one species produce fertile offspring. Because zorses cannot reproduce, horses and zebras are separate species. An infertile hybrid cannot form a new species because it cannot breed.

questions.question: Why did the proportion of dark peppered moths increase in industrial areas in the 1800s?
options: Soot caused pale moths to mutate into dark moths
Dark moths were better camouflaged on sooty bark, so more survived to breed
Moths changed colour to match the trees
Dark moths could fly faster
markScheme: 1 mark: dark moths camouflaged, so more survived to breed
questions.explanation: The dark variant already existed. On blackened bark birds saw and ate more pale moths, so dark moths survived and passed on the dark allele. Moths do not change colour to match their surroundings.

questions.question: Which of these could NOT be involved in evolution by natural selection?
options: An allele for thicker fur
A mutation that gives resistance to a disease
A scar gained in a fight
An allele that gives better camouflage
markScheme: 1 mark: a scar gained in a fight
questions.explanation: Evolution involves inherited characteristics. A scar is acquired during life and is not passed on in the gametes, so it cannot be selected for.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly describes natural selection?
options: Need for change → mutation → survival → reproduction
Variation → individuals change → offspring inherit the change
Survival → mutation → variation → reproduction
Variation → best suited survive → they breed → alleles become more common
markScheme: 1 mark: variation → best suited survive → they breed → alleles become more common
questions.explanation: Variation exists first. Mutations are random and do not happen because of a need. Individuals do not change and pass on those changes; instead the best suited survive and pass on alleles they already had.

questions.question: After Clean Air Acts reduced pollution, the proportion of pale peppered moths increased again. What is the best explanation?
options: Dark moths mutated back into pale moths
Pale moths were better camouflaged on cleaner bark, so they survived and bred more
Birds stopped eating moths
Clean air directly changed the moths' alleles
markScheme: 1 mark: pale moths better camouflaged on clean bark, so more survived and bred
questions.explanation: The selection pressure (predation by birds) reversed when bark became paler. The environment does not change alleles directly and moths do not mutate on demand.

questions.question:
A student collected a sample of peppered moths.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the percentage of dark moths in the sample.

Table 1 shows the percentage of peppered moths in a city that were dark.
Calculate the mean change in the percentage of dark moths per year between 1850 and 1900.
Give your answer in percentage points per year.

headers: Percentage of moths that were dark

markScheme: 1 mark: change = 90 − 2 = 88 percentage points over 50 years
questions.explanation: The increase is 88 percentage points over 1900 − 1850 = 50 years, so 88 ÷ 50 = 1.76 percentage points per year.

questions.question:
A species of bacterium divides every 30 minutes in ideal conditions.
Calculate the number of generations produced in 24 hours.
markScheme: 1 mark: 24 hours = 1440 minutes
questions.explanation: 24 × 60 = 1440 minutes; 1440 ÷ 30 = 48 generations. So many generations so quickly is why evolution can be seen in bacteria within days.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the numbers of green and brown beetles in a population at the start of a study and ten generations later.
Calculate the increase in the percentage of green beetles in the population.
questions.answerLabel: Increase in percentage of green beetles
markScheme: 1 mark: increase = 75 − 20 = 55 (percentage points)
questions.explanation: Work out each percentage from its own total: 40/200 = 20% and 300/400 = 75%. The increase is 55 percentage points. Comparing numbers alone would mislead because the population size changed.

questions.question:
One generation of a species of mouse lasts about 0.25 years.
Estimate the number of generations in 2000 years.
questions.explanation: Number of generations = total time ÷ generation time = 2000 ÷ 0.25 = 8000. Short generation times give natural selection more opportunities to change a population.

questions.question: State what the theory of evolution by natural selection says all species have evolved from.
markScheme: 1 mark: simple life forms (that first developed more than three billion years ago)
questions.explanation: All species have evolved from simple life forms that first developed more than three billion years ago.

questions.question: Give one selection pressure that could affect which rabbits in a population survive.
markScheme: 1 mark: any one, e.g. predators, disease, competition for food, cold weather
questions.explanation: Selection pressures are environmental factors that mean some individuals are more likely to survive than others.

questions.question: State what must happen to two populations of one species for them to have formed two new species.
acceptedAnswers: can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring
markScheme: 1 mark: they become so different (in phenotype) that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring
questions.explanation: Once two populations can no longer produce fertile offspring together, they are separate species.

questions.question: Explain why evolution is described as a change in a population rather than in an individual.
acceptedAnswers: alleles become more common in the population
markScheme: 1 mark: an individual's inherited characteristics/genes do not change during its life
1 mark: evolution is the change in the proportion (frequency) of alleles in a population over many generations
questions.explanation: Natural selection changes which individuals survive and breed, so the mix of alleles in the next generation changes. No individual organism evolves.

questions.question: Arctic foxes have thick white fur. Explain how natural selection could have led to all arctic foxes having white fur.
markScheme: 1 mark: variation in fur colour existed (due to mutation)
1 mark: white foxes were better camouflaged (could catch prey or avoid predators), so more likely to survive
1 mark: survivors bred and passed on the allele for white fur, which became more common over many generations
questions.explanation: The answer follows the chain: variation, advantage, survival, reproduction, inheritance of alleles over many generations.

questions.question: A student writes: 'Giraffes grew long necks because they stretched to reach high leaves, and they passed this on to their young.' Explain what is wrong with this statement.
markScheme: 1 mark: characteristics acquired during life (stretching) do not change the genes/are not inherited
1 mark: giraffes with naturally longer necks (genetic variation) were more likely to survive and pass on their alleles
questions.explanation: Evolution by natural selection acts on existing genetic variation. A characteristic gained by use during life is not passed to offspring.

questions.question: Suggest why evolution of antibiotic resistance in bacteria can be observed within a few years, while evolution in elephants takes much longer.
markScheme: 1 mark: bacteria reproduce very quickly (short generation time) / large numbers
1 mark: so many generations pass in a short time, allowing alleles to spread quickly (elephants have few generations in the same time)
questions.explanation: Natural selection acts once per generation. Bacteria may divide every 20 to 30 minutes, whereas an elephant generation lasts many years.

questions.question:
A farmer used the same pesticide on a crop for 12 years.
Table 1 shows the percentage of insect pests killed by the pesticide.
Explain the trend shown in Table 1.
markScheme: 1 mark: a mutation gave some insects resistance to the pesticide (variation)
1 mark: pesticide kills non-resistant insects; resistant ones survive and reproduce
1 mark: they pass on the resistance allele, so over many generations most of the population is resistant
questions.explanation: The pesticide is a selection pressure. It does not cause the mutation; it removes non-resistant insects so the resistance allele becomes more common.

questions.question: Explain why a mutation that occurs in a skin cell of an animal cannot contribute to the evolution of its species.
acceptedAnswers: only mutations in gametes are inherited
markScheme: 1 mark: the skin cell is a body cell, not a gamete (sex cell)
1 mark: so the mutation is not passed on to offspring / not inherited
questions.explanation: Evolution is a change in inherited characteristics. Only mutations in cells that form gametes can be passed to the next generation.

questions.question: Two populations of a species of frog have been separated for a very long time. Describe a test that would show whether they have become two different species.
markScheme: 1 mark: try to breed frogs from the two populations together
1 mark: if they cannot produce offspring, or the offspring are infertile, they are different species
questions.explanation: The definition of a species is based on producing fertile offspring, so the test must check both whether offspring form and whether those offspring can reproduce.

questions.question: Describe how the theory of evolution by natural selection explains the large number of different species on Earth today.
markScheme: Indicative content: all species evolved from simple life forms that first developed more than three billion years ago; populations show variation caused by mutations; individuals best suited to their environment survive and breed; they pass on their alleles; over many generations inherited characteristics change; different environments select different characteristics; populations can become so different that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, forming new species; repeated over billions of years this produces many species.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear description of natural selection linked to the formation of new species and the long time scale.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, such as 'the best suited survive', with little link to new species.
questions.explanation: A full answer links the steps of natural selection to the formation of new species and to the very long time since life began.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the percentage of peppered moths near an industrial city that were dark.
Air pollution from coal burning was high from about 1850 until Clean Air Acts were introduced in the 1950s.
Use Table 1 and your knowledge of natural selection to explain the changes in the percentage of dark moths.

headers: Percentage of moths that were dark

markScheme: Indicative content: describe the trend with data (2% rising to 90% by 1900 and 95% by 1960, then falling to 20% by 2000); dark colour is caused by a mutation (variation already present); soot blackened bark and killed lichens; dark moths camouflaged on dark bark; birds (predators) ate more pale moths; dark moths more likely to survive and breed; passed on allele for dark colour; allele became more common over many generations; after Clean Air Acts bark became paler; pale moths now better camouflaged; dark moths eaten more; proportion of dark moths fell; this shows populations, not individuals, change; the environment changing reversed the selection pressure.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): uses data to describe both the rise and fall, and gives a full natural selection explanation for both, including camouflage, predation, survival, reproduction and passing on alleles.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes the trend and gives a partial explanation for at least one change, mentioning camouflage and survival.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): describes the trend, or gives simple statements about camouflage, with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Strong answers quote the data, then explain each change with the full natural selection chain, and recognise that the reversal came from a change in selection pressure after pollution fell.
